Contrastive stress is seen in the following examples: cika 'he chips', cakd 'he vomits', boca-t 'a fish (species)', bocdr 'a turtle', pdsa 'he arrived (going upriver away from speaker)', pasd 'salt lick'. ... 8.1. Primary Word Stress. Although primary word stress is not predictable in Guayabero — the syllable bearing primary word stress can occur word initially, medially, or finally with no cooccurrence restrictions — it always occurs on either the ultimate or penultimate syllable of the grammatical stem, thereby identifying the stem in speech. Furthermore, syllable-final consonant clusters occur only in stem-final syllables bearing primary stress, so the maximum expansion of a syllable is always associated with primary stress. El estado fonémico del acento se establece por los siguientes contrastes:² /pasá/ 'pantano' /pása/ 'llegar' /pehíw/ 'su gente' /péhiw/ 'sus cosas' /bɨtát/ 'caña hueca' /bútat/ 'en la hamaca' /nehéla/ 'nuevo' /nehelá/ 'su pelo (de usted)' /ámo/ 'tú deberías decir' /amá/ 'aquí está' /púka/ 'lago' /baká/ 'sembrado, chagra' /asá/ 'otro' /ǽsa/ 'anzuelo' [fn. 2:] En términos generales la anexión no afecta el acento. [...] [p. 54, 4.2:] La palabra fonológica se compone de una a cinco sílabas. Se marca con pausa posible, aumento de velocidad prenuclear, y un núcleo caracterizado por acento primario y tono alto simultáneo
new_statements.translation: 3. Stress. The phonemic status of stress is established by the following contrasts: /pasá/ 'swamp' /pása/ 'to arrive' /pehíw/ 'his people' /péhiw/ 'his things' /bɨtát/ 'hollow cane' /bútat/ 'in the hammock' /nehéla/ 'new' /nehelá/ 'your hair' /ámo/ 'you should say' /amá/ 'here it is' /púka/ 'lake' /baká/ 'garden plot' /asá/ 'other' /ǽsa/ 'fishhook'. [fn. 2:] In general terms affixation does not affect the stress. The authors suspended their research before they could define the conditions for the change in stress placement when it does occur. [p. 54:] The phonological word consists of one to five syllables. It is marked by potential pause, prenuclear increase in tempo, and a nucleus characterized by simultaneous primary stress and high pitch.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog record (Keels 1985 secs. 2.4/8.1: contrastive, not predictable): Waller & Waller establish phonemic stress by (near-)minimal pairs, including the very pair Keels uses (pasa 'llegar'/'he arrived' vs pasa 'pantano'~'salt lick'). They do not state Keels's final/penult window in words, but all 14 contrast items are final- or penult-stressed (e.g. nehela 'nuevo' penult vs nehela 'su pelo' final). Detail not in the catalog: sec. 4.2 defines the phonological word (1-5 syllables) by one nucleus with simultaneous primary stress and high pitch; its 5-syllable example /pihimelisdo?/ 'de nuevo' carries the nucleus on the third (antepenultimate) syllable, uncommented by the auth…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is phonemic (lexically contrastive), demonstrated by minimal and near-minimal pairs differing only in stress position; every example has stress on the final or the penultimate syllable, but no positional rule or window is stated. Each phonological word (1-5 syllables) has one nucleus bearing primary stress together with high pitch; affixation generally leaves stress in place, with some undescribed shifts.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated: only one 'acento primario' nucleus per phonological word is described; no secondary or rhythmic stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Footnote 2 (p. 52): affixation ('anexion') in general does not affect stress, but stress shifts do occur in some cases whose conditioning the authors could not determine before suspending fieldwork. p. 50 fn.: monosyllables are written with the accent mark only when a phonetic example requires it. Stress-conditioned allophony: [ɔ] for /o/ in unstressed syllables (p. 52), /d/ realised as a voiceless interdental fricative right after stressed vocoids and implosive [ɓ] in a stressed initial syllable before intervocalic glottal stop (pp. 49-50). Phrase level (4.3, p. 54): pitch patterns of the phonological phrase are predictable; in type-one phrases the pitch peak 'se marca posteriormente con acento'.
new_statements.identity_note: Guayabero (jiw), Guahiboan, spoken on the Guaviare river (Meta/Guaviare, Colombia); Tobar Ortiz 2000 maps the settlements Cano Ceiba, Barrancon, La Sal, Barranco Colorado, Mucuare, Laguna Barajas and notes an older vs younger speakers' pronunciation difference. Waller & Waller 1976 and Kondo 1998 are SIL-Colombia (Lomalinda) descriptions of the same language; no dialect split is at issue.

sources.quote: 'A pesar de que el acento primario de palabra no es predecible en guayabero -- la silaba que posee acento primario puede ocurrir al comienzo de la palabra, en el medio de esta, o al final, y no hay restricciones co-ocurrentes -- siempre se presenta, o bien en la ultima silaba, o en la penultima de la raiz gramatical, identificando en esta forma la raiz.' (Spanish original says 'raiz' = root where the 1985 English says 'grammatical stem'.)

sources.quote: No rule for stress placement is stated. The orthography section only notes that diphthongs 'por lo general se acentuan en la primera vocal' and that ph/th are aspirated 'en posicion inicial de una silaba acentuada'; headwords carry a written acute accent whose position varies lexically (buya 'flecha', jela vs. athi 'sainos', jalwek 'buscar', kaka 'oso perezoso', to'a 'mandar'), consistent with unpredictable stress within a final two-syllable window but not an explicit statement.
